title: AQA English Language Paper 1 Question 5: Creative Writing (2026 Format)
description: AQA Paper 1 Question 5 guide for 2026: 40 marks, the 24/16 split, planning, description, story openings, structure, vocabulary and technical accuracy.

children: Paper 1 Question 5 is worth 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). For the 2026 format, AQA clarified two important points. The descriptive option can be written from your own imagination rather than being tied to the supplied picture, and the narrative option asks for the opening of a story rather than a complete story.
The first decision: description or story opening?

Choose the option that gives you the clearest material, not the one that sounds more impressive. A successful description needs deliberate movement of focus and atmosphere. A successful story opening needs controlled character, setting, viewpoint and a developing situation; it does not need to race through an entire plot.
Plan for control, not quantity
Choose one central atmosphere, idea or tension.

Plan three or four stages of development. For description, this might be wide view → detail → interruption → changed view. For a story opening, it might be setting → character goal → disturbance → unresolved turn.
Choose a small bank of precise details and images. Avoid planning twenty devices.
Decide where sentence length, paragraphing and punctuation can genuinely control pace or emphasis.
A useful description structure
Establish a clear viewpoint: where is the observer and what can they notice?
Move focus deliberately rather than listing objects.
Develop sensory detail selectively; not every sentence needs all five senses.
Let the atmosphere change or deepen so the piece has progression.
End on an image, detail or shift that feels connected to the opening.
A useful story-opening structure
Introduce the setting and character efficiently.
Give the character an immediate want, concern or uncertainty.
Allow one event, discovery or interruption to change the situation.
Use dialogue only when it reveals character or moves the opening forward.
Stop at a point that creates meaningful expectation; you are writing an opening, not resolving the whole narrative.
Mini-example: controlled imagery

Instead of stacking similes, choose one image and develop it. “Rain stitched the street to the grey sky” creates a visual link. A later detail about headlights “tearing the stitches apart” could develop the same image and create cohesion. Reusing an image with variation is often more controlled than introducing a new metaphor in every sentence.
AO6 is nearly half the task

The 16 technical-accuracy marks mean spelling, punctuation, grammar, vocabulary and sentence control are not an afterthought. Ambitious writing that repeatedly loses sentence boundaries can sacrifice a substantial part of the available marks.
Use sentence variety because the meaning needs it, not simply to tick a box.
Check full stops and commas before searching for exotic punctuation.
Keep tense and viewpoint consistent unless a change is deliberate.
Use ambitious vocabulary precisely. An accurate ordinary word is better than a misused impressive one.
Leave time to reread for missing words, agreement errors and repeated punctuation mistakes.
Common mistakes
Trying to tell a beginning, middle and ending at high speed.
Writing a static description that becomes a catalogue of colours and sounds.
Forcing a memorised story onto a prompt it does not fit.
Using a rhetorical-device checklist instead of creating a coherent voice.
Ignoring paragraphing and sentence control while chasing vocabulary.
Final checklist
My piece has a clear central idea or atmosphere.
The structure changes or develops.
Details are selected, not piled up.
My narrative is an opening, not a rushed complete story.
I have checked sentence boundaries, spelling and punctuation.
